themes.name: Futility: breath and vapor
themes.line: The book's key word, hevel, and every verse that calls something futile or a pursuit of the wind.

note.title: Hevel: breath, vapor, futility
note.body: The book's key word appears dozens of times and describes the whole of life under the sun. Whether it is best heard as emptiness, brevity, or enigma, it names the experience of grasping at something that won't stay in the hand. The book does not say God's world is worthless; it says that nothing in it can bear the weight of being our ultimate gain.

themes.name: Nothing new under the sun
themes.line: Generations, sun, wind and rivers going round and round, and no one remembered.

themes.name: The Teacher's search
themes.line: A king tests pleasure, great works, wisdom and folly to see what is worthwhile, and reports what he found.

themes.name: Toil and what it gains
themes.line: Labor under the sun, what it earns, who inherits it, and the mind that does not rest at night.

themes.name: Eat, drink and enjoy: the gift of God
themes.line: Bread, wine, work and the people we love, received day by day as the portion God gives.

note.title: Joy as God's gift
note.body: Seven times the book commends eating, drinking, and finding satisfaction in work, and it calls these the gift of God. This is not despairing hedonism. It is the recognition that ordinary goods, received gratefully day by day, are the portion God gives, even when the larger meaning escapes us.

themes.name: Death comes to all
themes.line: One fate for the wise and the fool, the righteous and the wicked, people and animals.

note.title: Death, the great leveler
note.body: The Teacher returns again and again to death, which comes to the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, humans and animals alike. Death exposes the limits of every strategy for securing a legacy. The book forces the reader to face mortality honestly rather than distract from it.

themes.name: Wisdom and folly
themes.line: Wisdom is better than folly as light is better than darkness, and a little folly can spoil it.

themes.name: What no one can know
themes.line: The work of God that no one can fathom, the future no one can see, and time and chance.

note.title: The limits of wisdom
note.body: Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness, and the Teacher never denies it. But wisdom cannot see the whole of God's work, cannot straighten what is crooked, and cannot prevent death. The book teaches humility about what human understanding can achieve.

themes.name: A time for everything
themes.line: A season for every purpose, the right time and way, and the hour no one knows.

deeper.label: When You Are Waiting on God

themes.name: Oppression and injustice
themes.line: Tears with no comforter, wickedness in the place of judgment, and justice delayed.

themes.name: Wealth and what it cannot buy
themes.line: The love of money that is never satisfied, riches hoarded or lost, and wealth its owner cannot enjoy.

themes.name: Fear God
themes.line: Careful worship, vows kept, and the God who will bring every deed into judgment.

note.title: The fear of God and his judgment
note.body: Beneath the Teacher's questions runs the conviction that God is real, sovereign, and just, even when injustice seems to win. The fitting response is reverent fear, careful worship, and obedience, and the epilogue makes this the book's conclusion: God will bring every deed into judgment.

themes.name: Words, vows and listening
themes.line: Drawing near to listen, letting words be few, keeping vows, and the fool who multiplies words.

themes.name: Kings and those in power
themes.line: Living under a king, rulers who err, the wise youth, and the poor wise man no one remembered.

themes.name: What is better
themes.line: The Teacher's comparisons: a good name, the house of mourning, a patient spirit, and two rather than one.

themes.name: Youth, age and remembering your Creator
themes.line: Rejoice while you are young, remember your Creator before the days of darkness, and the poem of old age.

chapters.title: Futility of Futilities: Nothing New Under the Sun
chapters.summary: A narrator introduces the words of the Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, and his motto: everything is futile. A poem follows on the endless cycles of generations, sun, wind, and rivers, where nothing is new and nothing is remembered. Then the Teacher speaks for himself, describing how he set out to explore everything done under heaven with wisdom and found it all to be a pursuit of the wind, and wisdom itself a source of grief.

chapters.title: The King's Experiment with Pleasure and Work
chapters.summary: The Teacher tests pleasure, wine, and great building projects, acquiring houses, vineyards, gardens, servants, flocks, treasure, singers, and concubines. He denies himself nothing, yet finds it all futile. He then weighs wisdom against folly and finds wisdom better, but both the wise and the fool die and are forgotten. He comes to hate his toil, since he must leave its fruit to someone else, and ends by recognizing that the simple ability to eat, drink, and enjoy work comes from the hand of God.

chapters.title: A Time for Everything, and Eternity in the Heart
chapters.summary: The Teacher's famous poem lists fourteen pairs of opposites, a time to be born and a time to die, to weep and to laugh, to love and to hate. He reflects that God has made everything beautiful in its time and set eternity in human hearts, yet people cannot grasp the whole of God's work. He sees injustice in the courts, trusts that God will judge, and faces the hard fact that humans and animals share the same breath and the same dust.

chapters.title: Oppression, Envy, and the Strength of Two
chapters.summary: The Teacher looks at the oppressed, weeping with no one to comfort them, and finds the dead better off than the living. He sees that much labor springs from envy, meets a man who toils alone with no heir and no rest, and praises companionship: two are better than one, and a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. The chapter ends with a story of a poor, wise youth who replaces a foolish old king, only to be forgotten in his turn.

chapters.title: Few Words Before God, and the Emptiness of Wealth
chapters.summary: The Teacher turns from what he has seen to how a person should come before God: listen more than you speak, keep your vows, and fear God. He then observes layers of officials who exploit the poor, and he shows how the love of money never satisfies, how riches can be hoarded or lost, and how everyone leaves the world as naked as they came. He ends by commending the simple enjoyment of food, drink, and work as God's gift.

chapters.title: Having Everything and Enjoying Nothing
chapters.summary: The Teacher describes a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, yet who is not allowed to enjoy them, and he judges that a stillborn child is better off. Appetite is never satisfied, the wise have no final advantage over the fool, and no one can contend with the one stronger than he. The chapter ends with two questions no human can answer: what is good for a person in a fleeting life, and what will come after him.

chapters.title: What Is Better, and the Limits of Wisdom
chapters.summary: A string of proverbs tells what is better: a good name than perfume, mourning than feasting, patience than pride. The Teacher then observes that the righteous sometimes perish while the wicked live long, warns against extremes, and confesses that no one on earth is righteous without sin. He tried to be wise but found wisdom beyond reach, and his search yields only a few bitter findings, ending with this: God made people upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

chapters.title: Living Under Kings, and Justice Delayed
chapters.summary: The Teacher advises caution in the presence of a king whose word is supreme, and he observes that no one has power over the day of his death. He sees the wicked honored at their burials and notes that delayed justice encourages evil, yet he affirms that it will go well with those who fear God. Faced with a world where the righteous and the wicked often receive the opposite of what they deserve, he commends the enjoyment of life and concludes that no one, however wise, can comprehend the work of God.

chapters.title: One Fate for All, So Eat Your Bread with Joy
chapters.summary: The Teacher concludes that the righteous and the wise are in God's hands, yet the same fate, death, comes to everyone. Since the living still have hope and the dead have no share in life under the sun, he urges his reader to eat, drink, wear white, love his wife, and work with all his might. He observes that time and chance happen to all, and he tells the story of a poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten.

chapters.title: A Little Folly, and the Wisdom of Ordinary Life
chapters.summary: A collection of proverbs contrasts wisdom and folly in speech, work, and government. A little folly can spoil much wisdom, fools are promoted while the capable are passed over, everyday tasks carry hidden dangers, and skill makes work easier. The chapter warns about foolish words, lazy or self-indulgent rulers, and careless talk against those in power.

chapters.title: Cast Your Bread, Sow Your Seed, Rejoice in Your Youth
chapters.summary: The Teacher urges bold, generous action in the face of an uncertain future: cast your bread on the waters, divide your portion widely, and sow in the morning and evening, because no one knows which effort will succeed or what disaster may come. Light is sweet, so a person should rejoice in all his years while remembering the dark days ahead. The chapter ends with a call to young people to enjoy their youth, knowing that God will bring them to judgment.

chapters.title: Remember Your Creator, and the Whole Duty of Man
chapters.summary: The Teacher urges the young to remember their Creator before the days of old age and death arrive, which he describes in a haunting poem of a house falling silent, a lamp shattered, and dust returning to the ground while the spirit returns to God. The motto of the book returns: everything is futile. Then a second voice, the frame narrator, describes the Teacher's work and gives the conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments, for God will bring every deed into judgment.

reading: Read Ecclesiastes as a search, not a list of rulings. The Teacher often reports what he observed and felt at a given point, including conclusions he later qualifies, so a single verse lifted out (for example, that humans have no advantage over animals, 3:19) may not be the book's final word. Watch for the refrains: under the sun, a pursuit of the wind, nothing better than to eat and drink, and the key word hevel.

That word is the heart of the debate. Its basic meaning is vapor or breath. Some translations render it as vanity (the King James tradition) or meaningless (the New International Version), which stress emptiness. Others stress transience, life as a passing breath. Still others read it as enigma or absurdity, what cannot be grasped or made sense of; the scholar Michael V. Fox argued for absurd. The word may carry different shades in different places. Also watch the book's two voices: the Teacher, who speaks in the first person, and the narrator of the frame, whose closing words guide how we hear the rest.

hard.q: Is the Bible saying that life is meaningless?
a: Read on its own, verse 2 can sound like despair: everything is futile. But the key word, hevel, has a range of meanings. Some interpreters do take it as meaningless or empty, and they read the Teacher's words as an honest portrait of life without God that the book's frame then corrects. Others read hevel as transience: life is a breath, brief and fragile, not worthless but passing. Still others take it as enigma: life can't be figured out or mastered.

The phrase under the sun also matters. The Teacher is describing life as seen from within the world's own resources, and the book's frame narrator will close by pointing to the fear of God and his coming judgment (12:13-14). Most readers agree that the Bible is not saying that God's world or human life has no worth; it is saying that nothing under the sun can deliver the lasting gain we seek from it.

hard.q: Does the epilogue contradict the Teacher, or was it added to make a skeptical book acceptable?
a: Some scholars have argued that the epilogue was added by a later editor to soften a skeptical book and secure its place among the sacred writings. Others, including the scholar Michael V. Fox, have argued that the book was designed from the start as the words of the Teacher framed by a narrator, so that the epilogue belongs to its structure. Among those who see a frame, some think the narrator gently distances himself from the Teacher's more radical conclusions, and others think he endorses them, since he calls the Teacher wise and his words upright and true (12:9-10). Still others point out that the fear of God and God's judgment are not new ideas in the epilogue; the Teacher himself commanded the fear of God (5:7) and warned of judgment (3:17; 11:9). On this reading the conclusion does not overturn the Teacher's search but names where it was heading. The question of composition is open, but readers across these views agree that the book as it stands asks to be read with its conclusion.
